questions.scenario: A service gets 300 requests a second, each spending 1 second waiting on a provider.
questions.question: By Little's law, how many requests are in flight?
questions.explanation: In flight = arrival rate × time in the system.

questions.scenario: In the starter's benchmark at 300 requests/s with a 1 s provider, platform threads served 192/s with p50 2.98 s, while virtual threads and reactive served 279/s at about 1 s.
questions.question: Why?
options: Tomcat's 200-thread pool caps a 1-second call at about 200 requests a second, so the rest queued
Platform threads are slower at CPU work
questions.explanation: A blocking pool limits concurrency; virtual threads and reactive don't.

questions.scenario: At 200 requests/s, all three models had the same latency and no errors.
questions.question: What does that tell you?
options: Below the pool limit the threading model doesn't matter much; most services live there
questions.explanation: Differences show only past the limit, or at very high connection counts.

questions.scenario: The first benchmark runs had every variant failing half its requests at 500/s.
questions.question: What was the lesson?
options: The environment, not the frameworks, was the bottleneck: other services competed for CPU and the shared provider saturated first; check what a benchmark measures
questions.explanation: Load dependencies alone, check CPU, profile once.

questions.scenario: Under heavy overload, the virtual-thread service ran out of heap and stopped answering health checks.
questions.question: What's the right fix?
options: Add a limit on work in progress (a semaphore or bulkhead, or a gateway rate limit) so excess requests fail fast
Increase the heap until it stops
questions.explanation: Virtual threads remove the pool's accidental brake; put a deliberate one back.

questions.scenario: Which statement about virtual threads is accurate?
questions.question: Choose one.
options: They make waiting cheap: a blocked virtual thread unmounts and its carrier runs others
questions.explanation: They help I/O-bound concurrency, not computation.

questions.scenario: On Java 21, a virtual thread blocks on I/O inside a synchronized block in a hot path.
questions.question: What can happen, and what helps?
options: It becomes a platform thread forever
It pins its carrier thread, which can starve carriers; prefer ReentrantLock there, or use JDK 24+ where JEP 491 removed most pinning

questions.scenario: ITL Pay needs a service holding 20,000 open price streams to mobile apps.
questions.question: Which model fits best?
options: Platform threads with a pool of 20,000
Reactive (WebFlux with SSE), with backpressure per client
questions.explanation: Long-lived streaming connections are reactive's strength; request–response services suit virtual threads.
